opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think people underrate, because the replay buffer quietly defines what your agent's world actually is. Whatever's in there is the distribution you're optimizing over, so choosing what goes in is really choosing what the agent gets to care about.

The naive view is "put everything in, more data is better." That breaks down quickly with off-policy learning. If you fill the buffer with states your current policy would never visit, you spend a lot of capacity fitting Q-values in regions that don't matter. Worse, you can get bootstrapping errors: the critic is confidently wrong about actions it has never seen consequences for, and those errors propagate back through the Bellman backup. That's the classic offline RL problem, distribution shift between the data and the policy you're actually improving.

So my rough heuristic is that an off-policy state earns its place if it's informative about decisions your policy is plausibly going to face. A few categories pass that test.

First, near-misses and recoveries. States just off the nominal trajectory, where the robot slightly mis-grasped or the object slipped, are hugely valuable because that's exactly where a deployed policy drifts. Imitation learning taught us this the hard way. If you only train on perfect demonstrations, the policy has no idea how to get back once it makes a small error, and errors compound. Off-policy data that covers the recovery region is gold.

Second, states with diverse outcomes. If you have many transitions from roughly the same state with different actions and different results, you can actually learn the advantage of one action over another. A buffer full of single-action trajectories gives you very little contrastive signal.

Third, rare but consequential states, like failures, safety-critical moments, and sparse-reward successes. Those you often want to oversample rather than just include, because uniform sampling drowns them out.

What I'm more skeptical of is stale data from a much older policy in a regime the current policy has left behind. It isn't useless, but you should either down-weight it or use a method that's conservative about out-of-distribution actions. Otherwise you're asking the critic to extrapolate.

The deeper point, and the reason I think this matters for scaling, is that as we move toward big generalist models trained on huge heterogeneous datasets, the "replay buffer" starts to look a lot like the pretraining corpus. Data curation becomes the main lever. The algorithm matters, but deciding what experience is worth learning from is where much of the real leverage is.

r001.rationale: The response says that without training examples from recovery regions, the policy may not know how to recover from small errors, which then compound.

r002.rationale: It recommends including near-misses and recoveries from states where the deployed policy may drift.

r003.rationale: It says states the current policy would never visit can waste replay capacity and cause critic errors, but does not address the case where MCTS supplies optimal-action labels for those states.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that most of the time people don't think about it at all. They just keep everything, and the replay buffer is this big FIFO queue of whatever the policy happened to do in the last N million steps. And that works surprisingly well, which is part of why nobody questions it.

But if you actually think about what the buffer is for, the question becomes clearer. The buffer is a dataset, and you're training a function approximator on it. So the real question is: what distribution do you want your Q-function or your value function to be accurate on? And the answer is, you want it to be accurate on states your current policy is going to visit, plus a halo around that so that when the policy drifts, you're not falling off a cliff.

The states that are dangerous are the ones that are way off-policy in a way where the Bellman backup is going to be bootstrapping from actions the current policy would never take. That's where you get the extrapolation error that the whole offline RL literature is about. So one heuristic I like is: an off-policy state is worth keeping if the actions in that transition are still plausible under the current policy, or at least under some policy you'd be happy to evaluate. If the behavior policy that generated the data is now totally alien to you, that transition is mostly contributing noise to your targets.

The other thing I'd say is that the real-world robotics setting changes the calculus a lot. In simulation, data is free, so you can afford to be picky and just throw things away. In the real world, every transition cost you something, maybe a human teleoperator's time, maybe a broken gripper. So you really don't want to discard anything. And then the problem flips from "what do I keep" to "how do I weight it." You keep everything, but you reweight by how relevant it is to the current policy, something like a prioritized replay but where the priority is about distribution shift rather than TD error.

And honestly I think the field is moving toward treating this less like a buffer and more like a big foundation-model-style dataset. You collect everything, you never throw it out, and you let the model's capacity and the training recipe sort out what matters. The replay buffer as a sliding window was really an artifact of memory constraints on a single GPU in 2015. Once you take that constraint away, "which states belong" starts looking a lot like "which documents belong in a pretraining corpus," and the answer there has mostly been "all of them, but filtered for quality and deduplicated."

r001.rationale: The response discusses extrapolation error from bootstrapping on actions the current policy would not take, but does not explain compounding errors caused by lacking examples of how to return from off-policy states to the policy’s optimal state distribution.

r002.rationale: It says to keep transitions whose actions remain plausible under the current policy, but does not recommend including recovery trajectories from states the policy could plausibly drift into.

r003.rationale: The response says far off-policy states can be dangerous, but does not identify training on states the policy would never reach as harmful even when MCTS provides optimal-action labels.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful question is: which states would your current policy benefit from learning how to recover from? Because you can fill a replay buffer with all sorts of states, but being off-policy doesn’t by itself make them useful.

Imagine a robot trying to pick up a cup. If it bumps the cup and the cup tips over, that’s a pretty valuable state to keep. It’s a mistake the policy might actually make, and learning what to do next can make the whole behavior more robust. But if you put the robot in some completely arbitrary configuration that it would never encounter, you could spend a lot of learning capacity solving a problem that doesn’t improve the task.

There’s a tension, though, because you don’t want to restrict the buffer to what the current policy already does. Then you lose the experiences that could help it discover something better. So I’d want a mixture: states close to the current policy’s distribution, plausible failures, and some experiences that show a better path. The criterion is whether learning from those states improves the policy when you actually run it.

r001.rationale: The response says recovery examples can help, but does not explain compounding errors from lacking examples of returning to the policy’s optimal state distribution.

r002.rationale: It recommends keeping plausible failures the policy might encounter and learning what to do next from them, which conveys including recovery experience from plausible drift states.

r003.rationale: It says arbitrary states the policy would never encounter can waste learning capacity, but does not address MCTS providing optimal-action labels for those states.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: off-policy with respect to what? A state can be unlikely under your current policy and still be very useful to learn from. Maybe it’s a state you’ll encounter once your policy gets better, or it’s a failure state that you want the policy to learn how to recover from.

In robotics, for example, if you only train on trajectories where the robot is successfully grasping an object, then when it knocks the object over, it has no idea what to do. Keeping those messy states in the buffer can be valuable. But you can also fill a buffer with situations that your policy is never going to encounter, and spend all your learning capacity on those.

So I’d think about the buffer as defining a curriculum. You want some coverage of what the policy currently encounters, some memory of things it used to struggle with, and some states just beyond its current capabilities. And there’s a distinction between keeping a transition and sampling it frequently. You might want a broad archive, while changing the sampling distribution as the policy improves.

r001.rationale: The response says failure states can teach recovery, but does not explain compounding errors caused by lacking examples that return from off-policy states to the policy’s optimal state distribution.

r002.rationale: It recommends retaining messy failure states the robot could plausibly reach, such as after knocking an object over, so it can learn how to recover.

r003.rationale: It warns that training on situations the policy will never encounter can waste learning capacity, but does not address MCTS providing optimal-action labels for those states.
